status: candidate / pending_human_review (model reading of the candidate supporters against the operator-supplied revised statement, BRIEF_R22.md; not a gate decision)
statement_tested: VF-23 revised statement split into clauses C1-C4 (BRIEF_R22.md). C1: connectivity, graph/network or complexity measures discriminate MCI from controls in the study's own data. C2: within the same study such a measure separates MCI where spectral band-power does not. C3: report every within-study, same-participant head-to-head of discrimination between feature domains and its direction. C4: within the same study a multi-domain combination (spectral plus complexity and/or connectivity) discriminates MCI better than any single domain.

results.C3_head_to_head: Yes, and it goes against the clause's rival reading. The same MCI and HC participants go through the same random-forest pipeline: covariates residualised, SMOTE, GridSearchCV, one 80/20 stratified test split, AUC. MCI vs HC: EEG relative PSD 0.76, dwPLI FC 0.49 (chance), PSD+FC 0.59. Spectral band power beats connectivity for MCI, and adding connectivity lowers the AUC. No AUC-difference test and no CIs; the test set holds at most about 10 MCI. Other stages, same pipeline: SCD vs HC, PSD 0.69 and FC 0.68 (combined 0.78); AD vs HC, FC 0.77 beats PSD 0.68 (combined 0.84).
results.dataset_family: Shenzhen People's Hospital + Shenzhen BGI Life Sciences Research Institute multimodal cohort (ChiCTR2300074261): 168 HC, 30 SCD, 51 MCI, 28 AD; EEG available for a subset (Fig. 1B). Not ADNI or any public set.
results.method_family: 64-channel eyes-closed rsEEG: relative PSD (Welch, 7 bands) and debiased wPLI functional connectivity on the Desikan-Killiany atlas. Covariate ANOVA screen, then pairwise Wilcoxon group maps at uncorrected p<0.05. Random forest per modality and per combination alongside genomics, metagenomics, metabolomics and MRI volumes.
results.independence_note: No site, cohort or author overlap with the current supporters: P-553 (Hanyang, Korea), P-501 (Detroit/MADRC), P-463 (Valladolid analysis of two Japanese hospitals' MEG) and P-480 (PREVIEW, Florence). It shares a funding grant number (MOST 2022ZD0211600) with round-21 candidate P-552, with no shared site or authors. Not in registry_duplicates.json.
results.why: Identity: the PDF title, first author (Lin), DOI 10.1002/alz.70182 and the 277-participant design match the Paper 1322 block and registry row. Whole text read. C1 partly: the MCI-HC dwPLI differences exist only as edge-wise pairwise Wilcoxon tests at p<0.05. No multiplicity correction is stated, across more than 2,000 atlas region pairs (Desikan-Killiany plus subcortical structures) x 7 bands (Fig. 6 caption). The authors call MCI the group with 'the fewest changes in FC'. The FC classifier for MCI vs HC is at chance (AUC 0.49). So connectivity 'discriminates' MCI only in uncorrected group maps, not in classification. C2 partly: at the group-map level the pattern is there, with PSD showing no significant MCI-HC change in any band while some FC edges do. But both maps are uncorrected, the FC map has far more tests, and the study's own discrimination analysis reverses the pattern (PSD 0.76 vs FC 0.49). C4 no, for MCI: PSD+FC (0.59) is worse than PSD alone (0.76), and the text says 'adding FC did not improve performance'. The multi-domain gain appears only in other populations: SCD vs HC, where combined 0.78 beats 0.69/0.68, and AD vs HC, where combined 0.84 beats 0.68/0.77. Those are not MCI results, and the MCI result runs against the clause. Caveats: one 20% test split with at most about 10 MCI (fewer if EEG was missing, Fig. 1B); AUCs untested; age inclusion 20-70; MCI is clinical ('MCI due to AD' by MoCA<=26 and ADL), with no biomarker; the HC group is much larger than MCI (168 vs 51) and is balanced by SMOTE. Block gap: the summary block records neither the PSD/FC group results nor the per-domain AUCs. Net for VF-23: counter-evidence on C3 and C4 for MCI; a weak, uncorrected echo of C1/C2 at group level only.

quotes.quote: Notably, in MCI subjects, no significant changes in PSD were observed across the examined frequency bands.

The MCI group exhibited the fewest changes in FC among the three cognitive decline groups compared to HC. The widespread theta band connectivity enhancement observed in SCD disappeared in MCI, replaced by significant reductions in FC within the frontal lobe. The most notable changes occurred in the gamma1 band, with significant enhancement concentrated within the temporal lobe and between the temporal lobe and subcortical structures.
Significant connections (p < 0.05) from the Wilcoxon rank-sum test are marked by scatter dots
Topographic maps display significant mean differences (p < 0.05) in EEG relative power across frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, beta1, beta2, gamma1, gamma2) for three comparisons
EEG features maintained predictive power like that observed in SCD, with EEG relative PSD alone achieving an AUC of 0.76, although adding FC did not improve performance.
[Table 1, MCI versus HC; columns Precision, Recall, F1-score, Specificity, AUC] EEG relative PSD 0.77 0.79 0.78 0.91 0.76 / EEG FC 0.67 0.79 0.73 0.97 0.49 / EEG combined 0.87 0.85 0.8 1 0.59

Neuroimaging features showed more promise, with brain region volume, EEG relative PSD, and EEG FC achieving moderate performances (AUCs = 0.60, 0.69, and 0.68, respectively). The best predictive model combined EEG relative PSD and FC, reaching an AUC of 0.78.
with EEG PSD achieving an AUC of 0.68 and FC 0.77. Combining the two EEG features improved the AUC to 0.84.
The dataset was initially split into an 80% training set and a 20% test set using stratified sampling to ensure balanced class labels across splits.

An initial ANOVA was performed on relative power density and dwPLI, with age and education included as covariates, to identify significant alterations in power density and FC across brain regions. Following this, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to assess differences in PSD and FC among the four groups.

results.C3_head_to_head: Yes: complexity vs spectral in the same subjects (Dataset I, 29 MCI / 32 HC, Isfahan). Same spatial-tensor PARAFAC + RBF-SVM pipeline for every feature family, subject-wise random splits (41 train / 20 test) repeated 3 times, patch voting, accuracy only (Table 5, p.11). Power of 60 micro-bands 93.96%; 19 spectral features 83.37%; Shannon entropy 83.21%; Lempel-Ziv 82.75%; theta+alpha1 band power 82.13%; multiscale sample entropy 68.89%. Complexity does not outperform spectral: fine-band power is clearly best, conventional spectral sets roughly tie LZ and Shannon entropy, and MSE is worst. No significance test. The comparison leans toward spectral, because the time patch and the frequency segmentation were tuned on power features using the same data (Tables 2-3), and the number of PARAFAC components was picked per method by best accuracy. Dataset II (Emotiv, 20/20) tested spectral features only.
results.dataset_family: Dataset I: Noor Hospital, Isfahan rsEEG set (the Kashefpour et al. 2019 dataset, the paper's ref. [24]); 61 participants over 55 (29 MCI, 32 HC by MMSE 21-26 vs >26, NUCOG confirmation); 19-channel EB-Neuro, 30 min eyes closed. Dataset II: 14-channel Emotiv Epoc set (ref. [32]), 20 MCI / 20 HC, spectral features only. The authors do not have permission to share the data. No overlap with any VF-23 supporter's dataset.
results.method_family: 19-channel rsEEG features (absolute band power, 19 spectral features, 40/60/80 micro-band powers; Lempel-Ziv complexity, Shannon entropy, multiscale sample entropy) projected onto a 5x5 electrode grid to form a spatial tensor; PARAFAC decomposition; RBF SVM; subject-wise random train/test splits x3 with voting over time patches.
results.independence_note: Iran University of Science and Technology / New Zealand College of Chiropractic authors. The dataset is independent of P-553, P-501, P-463 and P-480. Not in registry_duplicates.json.
results.why: Identity: the summary block (headed with the file name 1-s2.0-S240584402402396X-main.pdf) carries the title 'A tensor decomposition scheme for EEG-based diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment' and the authors Faghfouri, Shalchyan et al., and these match the PDF (Heliyon 10 (2024) e26365). Whole text read. C1 yes: three complexity measures (LZ 82.75%, Shannon entropy 83.21%, MSE 68.89%) classify held-out MCI vs HC subjects above chance in the study's own data (Table 5). The caveats are substantial. There is accuracy only, with no CI or test. Each repeat has only 20 test subjects. Hyperparameters (time patch, frequency segmentation, number of components R) were selected on accuracy in the same data, so every figure is optimistic. MCI is defined by MMSE 21-26. There is also a minor inconsistency on the training set (41 subjects on p.4, '67% of people (40 people)' on p.10). C2 no: no spectral measure fails where a complexity measure succeeds, since every spectral feature set classifies at least as well. C3: a head-to-head exists and favours spectral features (above). C4 not tested: no model combines spectral and complexity features. Block gap: the block reports only the tensor-vs-conventional headline, not the feature-family comparison in Table 5.

results.C3_head_to_head: Yes, but only on a prognostic comparator (31 progressive vs 41 stable MCI at 2 years; no controls), in the same patients. Classification accuracy is in-sample, from logistic regression adjusted for age, sex and MMSE, at a 50% threshold: GFP theta (spectral global field power) 74.6%, GFS beta (global field synchronization, a global phase-synchronization measure) 67.6%, CSF neurogranin 70.0% (Table 5, PDF p.7). Group t-tests point the same way: GFP delta p=0.032 and theta p=0.003, with no GFS band different (PDF p.5). Direction: spectral beats synchronization. The accuracy difference is not tested and there is no cross-validation.
results.dataset_family: Karolinska University Hospital-Huddinge memory clinic cohort (Stockholm): 99 MCI (Winblad criteria), 72 with at least 2 years of follow-up (41 stable, 31 progressive to AD dementia); 19-channel eyes-closed rsEEG plus CSF.
results.method_family: 19-channel rsEEG: global field power (spectral amplitude, root mean across channels) and global field synchronization (Koenig) in 4 bands. Independent t-tests. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex and MMSE, with in-sample classification accuracy. Combined with CSF neurogranin.
results.independence_note: Swedish single-site cohort, independent of P-553, P-501, P-463 and P-480; no author overlap. Not in registry_duplicates.json.
results.why: Identity: the PDF title 'Synaptic Molecular and Neurophysiological Markers Are Independent Predictors of Progression in Alzheimer's Disease' (Smailovic et al., JAD 83 (2021) 355-366, DOI 10.3233/JAD-201234) matches the Paper 511 block and the registry row. Whole text read; ligature glyphs are normalised to 'fi' in the quotes. Every result is progressive vs stable MCI. No non-impaired comparator exists, so nothing here can be a full 'yes' on the MCI-vs-control clauses. C1 partly (different comparator): GFS beta is a significant predictor of progression only in the covariate-adjusted logistic regression (p=0.043, 67.6%). There is no GFS group difference in t-tests. C2 no: the pattern is reversed. Spectral GFP separates progressive from stable MCI (delta p=0.032, theta p=0.003) while no GFS measure does. C4 partly (different comparator; confounded with CSF): every combination tested includes CSF neurogranin, and no EEG-only GFP+GFS model is reported. Adding GFS beta to neurogranin + GFP theta raised in-sample accuracy from 74.3% to 81.4%, and GFS beta stayed significant in that three-predictor model (p=0.039; OR 1.446, 95% CI 1.019-2.051). The best combination (81.4%) beats every single predictor (best 74.6%). So connectivity adds information beyond spectral power, but only inside a CSF-containing prognostic model, in-sample, with one more parameter and no test of the accuracy gain. The paper reports GFP theta alone as 74.6% in Table 5 but '74.3%' in the text (PDF p.8). Four GFP-alpha outliers and one neurogranin outlier were excluded. The finder's 'same 99 MCI patients' is inexact: the prognostic analyses use the 72 with follow-up.

quotes.quote: Two qEEG measures of global field power (GFP) and global field synchronization (GFS) were computed in four conventional frequency bands: delta (1-3.5 Hz), theta (4-7.5 Hz), alpha (8-11.5 Hz), and beta (12-19.5 Hz).

The differences in baseline qEEG power measures included significantly higher GFP in delta (p = 0.032) and theta frequency band (p = 0.003) in progressive compared to stable MCI patients (Fig. 1). There were no statistically significant differences in GFS measures between stable and progressive MCI groups.

revealed that CSF neurogranin (p = 0.023), GFP theta (p = 0.026), and GFS beta (p = 0.043) were all significant predictors of progression to AD dementia in MCI patients during two years follow-up. GFP theta as a single predictor demonstrated the highest classification accuracy (74.6%) compared to CSF neurogranin (70.0%) and GFS beta alone (67.6%) (Table 5).
[Table 5] CSF Ng & GFP theta 1.010 2.424 74.3% ... CSF Ng & GFP theta & GFS beta 1.009 2.841 1.446 81.4% (1.000-1.017)* (1.184-6.819)* (1.019-2.051)* ... All models controlled for age, sex, and MMSE.

however, the classification accuracy remained the same as for GFP theta alone (74.3%). On the other hand, combination of CSF neurogranin with GFS beta and either GFP delta (p = 0.030 for CSF neurogranin, p = 0.043 for GFP delta, p = 0.0497 for GFS beta) or GFP theta (p = 0.038 for CSF neurogranin, p = 0.019 for GFP theta, p = 0.039 for GFS beta) displayed higher classification accuracy than either of these markers alone, with the latter combination reaching 81.4% (Table 5).
Classification accuracy, using a threshold of 50% for predicted probabilities, was used to quantify correctly categorized progressive versus stable MCI.

results.C3_head_to_head: Yes, but only on a prognostic comparator (64 MCI who progressed to AD vs 53 stable MCI; no controls in the main analyses), in the same patients. Stand-alone models share one stacking pipeline with fixed 10x repeated 10-fold CV splits (p.13). Sensor covariance (power on the diagonal plus cross-sensor terms) AUC 0.74 (SD 0.13); power-envelope correlation 0.71 (SD 0.15); dwPLI 0.67 (SD 0.15). There is no pure-power stand-alone model and no test of these AUC differences, and the SDs overlap widely. Univariate tests point the same way: averaged power differs at 16-40 Hz [T2 p<0.05], while averaged AEC and dwPLI are null after correction and differ only in the multivariate Riemannian MANOVA. Direction: the power-bearing measure is at least as good as the coupling measures. Connectivity does not outperform.
results.dataset_family: BioFIND (MRC CBU Cambridge + CTB Madrid, Elekta 306-channel MEG, controlled access via DPUK): 117 MCI with follow-up (64 progressive, 53 stable); MRI for 104. Registry stub P-577 is a duplicate of P-488 and must not be counted separately.
results.method_family: Resting eyes-closed MEG (102 magnetometers), Morlet wavelets 1-64 Hz: power, covariance, power-envelope correlation, dwPLI. TFCE cluster permutation and Riemannian distance MANOVA. Logistic regression with clinical and MRI covariates. Stacked ridge/logistic classifier with 10x10-fold CV and conditional permutation importance.
same_sample_or_cohort_as: P-577 (registry duplicate stub of this paper)
results.independence_note: Paris / Roche Basel / Madrid / Cambridge authors. No author overlap with P-463 (Rodriguez-Gonzalez, Nunez, Gomez, Hoshi, Shigihara, Hornero, Poza) or the other supporters. The BioFIND dataset is independent of all four supporters.
results.why: Identity: the PDF title 'Exploring the neuromagnetic signatures of cognitive decline from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease dementia' (Gaubert et al., eBioMedicine 2025;114:105659) matches the Paper 488 block and registry row. Whole text read up to the reference list. All main results compare progressive with stable MCI. The only MCI-vs-control comparison (BioFIND controls vs MCI, supplementary Figs S6/S8, described on p.17) is power-only, so it cannot address connectivity. C1 partly (different comparator): the coupling measures classify progression above chance in CV (AEC 0.71, dwPLI 0.67), and Riemannian MANOVA finds FDR-significant differences (AEC 2.3-64 Hz; dwPLI 9.2-9.8 and 45.3-46.9 Hz). Univariate averaged AEC and dwPLI are not significant after correction. The authors decline to interpret AEC and dwPLI as functional connectivity because they are sensor-space measures (p.6). C2 no: spectral power itself separates the groups (16-40 Hz by T2; 9.5-62 Hz posterior sensors by T3), so there is no case where a coupling measure separates the groups and power does not. The authors do say covariance MANOVA found low-frequency (1-4 Hz) differences 'not consistently detectable based on pure sensor space power' (p.16). But that measure contains power on its diagonal, the advantage comes from a multivariate test that was never applied to power alone, and the comparator is progression. It is a methods-sensitivity point, not a connectivity-over-power dissociation. C4 no (different comparator in any case): the only combined model is 'all inputs' (MEG covariance, AEC, dwPLI, MRI, age, sex, education, MMSE, site), AUC 0.81. Conditional permutation importance credits that model to MEG covariance, MMSE, MRI and site, not to dwPLI or power envelopes. The authors state the model 'did not gain added information from dwPLI and power envelopes', and no MEG-only multi-domain model is reported. Other caveats: site is partly collinear with progression (CBU 23/27 progressors); follow-up duration is undocumented per patient; AD diagnosis is clinical, without CSF or PET; the power-feature choice for the logistic regression was made after exploring the data (the authors acknowledge the circularity risk).

quotes.quote: We used a subset of 117 of the patients with MCI in BioFIND who had follow-up data. Of these, 64 subsequently progressed to probable AD dementia based on clinical criteria according to McKhann et al. (2011)60 (AD progression group), whereas 53 remained stable (stable MCI).

The covariance between sensors at a given frequency provides an extension of spectral power as it includes the power spectrum (diagonal term of covariance) but also provides information about the correlation between sensors (cross terms).
AD progression was associated with reduced averaged spectral power compared to stable MCI in frequencies ranging from 16Hz to 40Hz [T2: p < 0.05] (Fig. 1a-c).

Results were not statistically significant following permutation F-test [T2] with multiple-comparison correction across all frequencies (Fig. 3c and 4c). However, Riemannian-distance MANOVA [T4] offered a different picture: for power-envelope correlations, we observed significant effects along the entire frequency spectrum (Fig. 3d); for dwPLI, we observed two significant frequency ranges, one above 8Hz and one above 40Hz (Fig. 4d).

MEG dwPLI was the weakest among the brain models (AUC = 0.67, SD = 0.15). MEG power envelopes showed improvements but higher variance (AUC = 0.71, SD = 0.15). The best marginal performance was observed for MEG covariances (AUC = 0.74, SD = 0.13) and MRI cortical volumes (AUC = 0.77, SD = 0.14). Combining all inputs led to markedly improved classification scores (AUC = 0.81, SD = 0.12), suggesting synergies between the different modalities.
revealed that the full model relied on MEG covariances, MMSE, MRI and site (Fig. 5b).

Importantly, the data-driven classification model performed effectively when based solely on covariance features, suggesting potential redundancy between covariance, dwPLI, and power envelope metrics. However, that the model did not gain added information from dwPLI and power envelopes does not mean that these metrics do not, in principle, provide complementary information but could, rather, be due to the small size of the dataset.

An important finding is that covariance matrices analysed with Riemannian methods exhibited significant differences between groups across a wider range of frequencies than spectral power alone, particularly in the lower range of 1-4Hz, suggesting higher sensitivity of covariance versus power to identify future decliners.

In this work, we therefore refrained from an interpretation of the power-envelope and dwPLI metrics in terms of functional connectivity, which, for proper interpretation, requires anatomical source modelling.

summary: None of the four candidates gives within-study evidence that connectivity or complexity measures outperform spectral band power. Every head-to-head found goes the other way or ties. P-1322 (MCI vs HC): PSD AUC 0.76 vs dwPLI 0.49. P-153 (MCI vs HC): fine-band power 93.96% vs complexity at best 83.21%. P-511 (progressive vs stable MCI): GFP theta 74.6% vs GFS beta 67.6%. P-488 (progressive vs stable MCI): covariance 0.74 vs AEC 0.71 vs dwPLI 0.67. None of these differences is statistically tested. C1: P-153 yes (complexity classifies MCI vs HC, with optimistic tuning); P-1322 partly (uncorrected group maps only); P-511 and P-488 partly (prognostic comparator). C2: P-1322 partly, at the uncorrected group level only and reversed by its own classifier; the other three no. C4: no clean support. P-1322 is counter-evidence for MCI (combined 0.59 < PSD 0.76) and supports it only in SCD and AD. P-511 is partly, inside a CSF-containing prognostic model. P-488 is no. P-153 does not test it.
